translation_updates.summary: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose 1905 and 1915 papers established special and general relativity, transforming twentieth-century understanding of space, time, and gravitation. He also made significant contributions to quantum theory, and the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized his services to theoretical physics and, in particular, his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect rather than relativity itself. A body of historical scholarship has traced anticipations of relativity's mathematics in earlier work by Hendrik Lorentz and Henri Poincaré, but mainstream historians of science credit Einstein with the conceptual break — eliminating the ether and establishing the relativity of space and time — that the theory required. He worked in Berlin until 1933 and then emigrated to the United States, where he remained until his death in 1955.

Rudolf Clausius was a German physicist and mathematician described as one of the central founding figures of the science of thermodynamics, a status tied specifically to his reworking of Sadi Carnot's principle into what the source calls a firmer basis for the theory of heat. His 1850 paper on the moving force of heat first set out the basic ideas of the second law of thermodynamics. In 1865 he originated the concept of entropy, giving it its first mathematical formulation and coining the term itself from the Greek word for transformation. He later extended kinetic theory by incorporating rotational and vibrational molecular motion into earlier, simpler gas models.

Ludwig Boltzmann was an Austrian mathematician and theoretical physicist who developed statistical mechanics and supplied the statistical explanation of the second law of thermodynamics. In 1877 he formulated what became the standard statistical definition of entropy, expressing it in terms of the number of microstates available to a system. Statistical mechanics as a field is generally credited not to Boltzmann alone but to three physicists working from the 1870s onward — Boltzmann, James Clerk Maxwell, and Josiah Willard Gibbs. Boltzmann spent much of his career at the University of Graz before returning to the University of Vienna, where he succeeded his own teacher Josef Stefan as professor.

Rudolf Virchow was a German physician and scientist whose 1858 work Cellular Pathology is regarded as foundational to modern pathology. In it he articulated the third tenet of cell theory — that all cells arise from pre-existing cells — building on and popularizing an idea that historians now widely regard as having been taken without credit from Robert Remak's earlier work on cell division. Virchow was one of the first to accept Remak's demonstration that new cells form through division rather than spontaneous generation, even though he had initially resisted it. Beyond cell theory, he founded the fields of cellular and comparative pathology and developed a systematic method of autopsy that still underlies modern practice.

Girolamo Fracastoro was an Italian physician, poet, and scholar active in Verona and Padua in the first half of the sixteenth century. In 1546 he proposed that epidemic diseases spread through transferable ‘seeds’ or minute particles capable of transmission by direct contact, by contact with contaminated objects, or across distance through the air, an account he set out across a three-part treatise on contagion. Later scholarship treats this account as an early precursor to germ theory rather than its founding statement, crediting Fracastoro with only basic forms of the idea, which Marcus von Plenciz expanded on more than two centuries afterward. He is also remembered for the 1530 poem that gave syphilis its name.

The theory of relativity comprises two related physics theories authored by Albert Einstein — special relativity, published in 1905, and general relativity, developed between 1907 and 1915 and finalized in 1916. Special relativity addresses the structure of spacetime in the absence of gravity, while general relativity extends this to describe gravitation and its role in cosmology and astrophysics. The theory superseded two centuries of Newtonian mechanics and introduced concepts such as four-dimensional spacetime, time dilation, and length contraction. Although Einstein's 1905 paper built on prior theoretical and empirical work by Hendrik Lorentz and Henri Poincaré, the historical debate over the theory's origins concerns the extent to which each contributor should be credited, not whether Einstein authored the theories himself.

notes: Editorial batch 9 — the public-surface half of session #60 Track G, for the five persons and one concept person-wave11-v1 added. Keeps the editorial gap at 0.

Regime: separated-context generation (ordered as Opus per decisions (26)/(76) — see the provenance correction below; it actually ran on claude-sonnet-5) grounded in the same fetch-corpus captures Track G QC used, then orchestrator machine QC + close-read. Machine: fetch-verify 27/27 PASS. Close-read: 6/6 = 100%.

Close-read found ZERO factual errors — the second batch running this session to need no correction on substance. Two specific biographical claims were spot-verified against the sources rather than assumed: the Clausius 1850 paper ("His most important paper, On the Moving Force of Heat, published in 1850, first stated the basic ideas of the second law of thermodynamics") and Virchow-s acceptance of Remak ("He was one of the first to accept the work of Robert Remak, who showed that the origin of cells was the division of pre-existing cells"). Both hold.

One patch, and it came from the generator-s own flag rather than from a QC catch: the theory-of-relativity summary closed with a clause calling relativity "a branch of theoretical physics", which the generator reported it could not source from the article — the only support was a category label, not prose. The underlying fact is real and live-verified in this session-s own person-wave11-v1 identity record (Wikidata P31 = Q4162444 branch of physics alongside Q3239681 scientific theory), but an editorial summary should not carry a clause its own citations cannot back. Clause removed; the rest of the sentence stands.

★ Generator self-restraint worth recording. It was told the Thermodynamics article credits Kelvin with the first concise definition of thermodynamics in 1854 — but that article was not in its supplied source set, so it declined to assert the comparison rather than cite a page it had not read. That is exactly the discipline the fabricated-source failure mode calls for, and it is the first time this session a generator refused an orchestrator-supplied fact for want of its own evidence.

It also caught two source-side defects: enwiki spells the same person "Josef Stefan" and "Joseph Stefan" in one article, and the Einstein priority material it was offered turns out to be a historian-s block quotation nested inside the article rather than the encyclopedia-s own voice. Neither changed a summary, both are recorded.

The batch-s most delicate attribution is Virchow-s third tenet of cell theory. The summary states it as widely regarded as taken from Robert Remak without credit, matching the stronger of the two sources while the generator deliberately consulted both ("widely recognized as being plagiarized" vs "it has been suggested"). This is consistent with the edge note on edge:rudolf-virchow-founded-cell-theory, which carries the same contest and holds confidence to 0.75.
Living-person check: all five persons deceased (Einstein 1955, Clausius 1888, Boltzmann 1906, Virchow 1902, Fracastoro 1553); decision (70) does not engage.

★ PROVENANCE CORRECTION 2026-07-29 (same session, after measurement). This batch was ordered with the Agent tool parameter model:"opus" and its notes originally claimed "Opus subagent" generation per decisions (26)/(76). THAT CLAIM WAS FALSE. Measured directly at session end with two minimal probes that asked a subagent to read its own model ID from its environment: a probe requesting model:"fable" returned claude-sonnet-5, and a probe requesting model:"opus" ALSO returned claude-sonnet-5. The per-call model override was inert for this entire session — env.CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="sonnet" in ~/.claude/settings.json is read at session start and wins over every per-call value, and removing it mid-session did not take effect. So editorial generation for this batch actually ran on claude-sonnet-5, not Opus. The orchestrator recorded the ORDER-s intent rather than the RUN-s fact, which is precisely the failure the proposal-generator contract already prevents by making the agent self-report proposed_by.model_version from its own environment. Editorial orders carried no such requirement; they now must.

★ Unintended A/B measurement, now the honest reading of this batch. Decision (26) measured editorial summaries at Opus 11/11 vs Sonnet 1/11, and decision (76) recorded editorial-on-Sonnet-5 as an explicitly UNMEASURED A/B candidate not to be adopted blindly. Because the override was inert, session #60-s four editorial batches were that A/B, run accidentally on Sonnet 5. Result as measured this session: batch 7 needed 4 patches including one factual error (Brentano-s Vienna professorship); batches 8, 9 and 10 needed zero substantive corrections, with the only batch-10 edit coming from the generator-s own flag. This is real evidence and it must not be read as an Opus result. It is also not yet a ratified routing change — decision (26)/(76) still stand until a CPO ruling, and n=4 batches from one session with a hardening order template is a weak basis on its own.
